Goddammit, and here I thought Durarara's cliffhanger was tough. I'm not usually in favor of deus ex machina's, but I really don't want Ayumi to die. Then again, she's the perfect character for death at this point. She's an adorable imouto with just enough personality and moe for the audience to love her, and her death/serious injury will have a deep, significant impact on the other characters. So I guess I'd like for her to die for the story, but would also like her to live because she's such a fun character.

While I'm glad that Jun Maeda has finally gotten around to starting the plot (no joke, if something hadn't happened this episode it would've been a drop), and for once it isn't Key Aids, I found that this week's episode highlighted yet another subtle, but important flaw Charlotte really struggles with:

Scene cuts.

Asai Yoshiyuki just does not know how to segue scenes. It's most visible in previous episodes with the awkward ending scenes, where Yuu would say something vague before the credits started - at the time, I thought it was just the show trying too hard to end on a "deep" note, but now I think it's just that the director doesn't know when to cut the scene, or how.

The two cuts that were most glaring this episode are the halfway-through advertisement cut and the ending. In the former, we go from a fairly well done conversation to a rather flat joke "That's a prerecorded show. Hah! [Cut]" It's 60 to zero! You can't go directly from dialogue to a cut, unless the dialogue is somehow related to the scene change - it's like stopping in the middle of a conversation. It's unnatural, it's noticeable, and it leaves you feeling blindsided.

And then, there's the episode ending. It's a cliffhanger! Drama! Suspense! Except it was sloppy as fuck. Specifically, a smooth pan across his face? If you're going to have a dramatic zoom in shot to build tension and imply suddenness and sharpness, you end the shot when the zoom is done - you don't linger! Reason being is that , the panning shot at the end completely defeats the purpose of the zoom technique. From the viewer's point of view, it's as if you're falling towards the ground, oh no, and then right before you hit the ground you just... hover there, for a bit. And then you hit. It's disorienting and just plain, poor animation.

I remember, when watching Zankyou no Terror, that one of my favorite things about the show, and one of its saving graces in fact, was how good the camerawork was. It followed conventional wisdom for cinematics - all but a very specific few rules for live-action cinematography apply to animation (and those are normally due to constraints of the mediums). Zankyou no Terror had all its fundamentals and technicalities polished to a shine, from the animation to the camera work to the voice acting (exception: "Yoor kidding"), but where it failed was on the grand scale - a shitty plot, lackluster pacing, and an inconsistent theme.

Charlotte, on the other hand, does the complete opposite - it has its grand design down pretty well, as Key works tend to, but almost all of its details are fucked up. The animation is top-tier, but it's undercut by terrible storyboarding. The voice acting is excellent, but it's sabotaged by poor dialogue and unmatched animation (see: Nao's really weird tone to Yuu's questioning mushroom drinks; it just doesn't match). And on, and on, and on.

Charlotte is like that one hyper talented kid who never learned the fundamentals of their sport. Sure, they can glide on talent for a bit, but once they reach the limit of their natural abilities the mistakes start to pile up to keep them from being truly great. Yet another "it had so much going for it, but..."
